stories.topic: The girl who learned to write on her mother's gravestone
stories.summary: Amit opens with a quiz, reading a passage he wrote. In early-nineteenth-century London, a man walks his young daughter to the churchyard at St Pancras, to the grave of her mother, who died of an infection days after giving birth to her. The girl traces the inscribed letters with her finger and learns to write that way. For years afterwards she returns alone to read beside the grave, carrying guilt that her birth killed her mother. Ajay guesses Mary Wollstonecraft, who is the mother. The girl is Mary Shelley. Amit admits the scene may be romanticised, but both women wrote books that changed the world.
stories.insight: The image sets up the episode: two outlaws, mother and daughter, linked by loss and by books, each radical in an age that wasn't ready for her.
stories.quote: She sits by the gravestone, and with a tiny slender finger solemnly traces the letters inscribed there, and this is how she learns to write.

stories.topic: Wollstonecraft meets Locke next door, and the backlash
stories.summary: Wollstonecraft was born in 1759 into a world where wives couldn't own property or initiate divorce and husbands could legally beat them. She was one of seven children of an alcoholic, violent father. Her escape came through a neighbour, Reverend Henry Clare, who introduced her to John Locke. There was no internet and few bookshops then, so you stumbled on such ideas by accident. Locke's language of equal rights for 'all men' made her ask where women stood. She answered Burke's defence of tradition and aristocracy with A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790), then wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). The reaction was scathing. Thomas Taylor mocked it with 'A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes', arguing that if women could have rights, so could animals. Horace Walpole called her a 'hyena in petticoats'.
stories.insight: One chance encounter with the right book can redirect a life. A principle's logic can also run further than its authors intended: Wollstonecraft simply took Locke's equality at face value, and that alone made her an outlaw.
stories.quote: And Wollstonecraft makes a jump that she looks at this line and goes, What the fuck do you mean all men are born equal?

stories.topic: Walking in the rain before jumping into the Thames
stories.summary: After an affair with a lover who proved unfaithful, and a child born outside marriage, a despairing Wollstonecraft decided to drown herself in the Thames. It was raining. She walked up and down for half an hour first so that her clothes would grow heavy and she would sink. Her suicide letter to the lover, reproduced in her collected letters, says she chose the Thames because no one who goes in comes out alive. A bystander saw her and rescued her. She later married the philosopher William Godwin and died eleven days after giving birth to their daughter. The cause was an infection Amit traces to a doctor who did not wash his hands.
stories.insight: Behind the famous treatise was a life of real torment, because being ahead of your time meant living without social cover. Her death also starts the thread of unwashed hands that the episode later pulls through Semmelweis.
stories.quote: She walks up and down for half an hour, so her clothes get heavy with the rain, and she's more likely to sink.

stories.topic: An eighteen-year-old invents science fiction with no template
stories.summary: Mary Godwin grew up in her father's intellectual salon and ran away with the already-married Percy Shelley. Around 1816 she sat by a fire with Shelley, Lord Byron and John Polidori, trading ideas for books. Polidori described the anatomist William Lawrence's lectures arguing there is no soul, only the body's organs. Percy, obsessed with Promethean themes, wondered whether humans had created God. Mary had grown up on Milton's Paradise Lost, and she fused these influences into Frankenstein. She was eighteen. Science fiction did not exist as a genre and she had no craft models, yet she told the story through three nested voices (a ship's captain, Frankenstein and the monster) in an age of omniscient narrators. The book was ignored, and people assumed her husband had written it. Percy contributed perhaps 4,000 of its 78,000 words, and Amit says those passages stand out as the bad writing.
stories.insight: Inventing without a template is a different order of achievement. The clumsiness and clichés modern readers notice are the marks of someone building the road as she walked it.
stories.quote: Here is someone writing without a model for a genre that does not exist, and just coming up with a miraculous book.

stories.topic: Semmelweis: the man who solved childbed fever and died in an asylum
stories.summary: Ignaz Semmelweis was born in 1818, the year of Frankenstein. He switched from law to medicine and in 1846 joined Vienna General Hospital as an obstetric assistant. One maternity ward had 10% mortality and the other 4%, and women begged to be kept out of the first. He ruled out overcrowding, since the safer ward was more crowded, and weather, since the wards were next to each other. The clue came when a colleague died after a scalpel nick with the same symptoms as childbed fever. Staff in Ward One also worked on corpses before examining mothers. Semmelweis made them wash in a chlorinated solution. Deaths fell from 18% in one recorded month to two percent, then one, and to zero within two years. But germ theory did not yet exist, so he could not explain why it worked, and he never published. Doctors took offence at being called unclean. He was sacked over departmental politics and had to move countries. In 1865 he was lured into an asylum, beaten by guards and locked in a straitjacket in a dark cell. He died two weeks later of a gangrenous arm.
stories.insight: Being right without a mechanism, in a way that insults the status of the people you must persuade, is a near-fatal combination. The story comes full circle: unwashed hands killed Wollstonecraft too.
stories.quote: But here's the thing, he solved the problem without knowing why.

stories.summary: One German physician Semmelweis reached actually accepted the handwashing finding. He then realised that a loved one, a cousin or similar, had died after he attended her without washing his hands. Understanding that he had unknowingly killed her, he took his own life. Ajay voices the reflex of the doctors who refused to listen: 'Am I being blamed for all the deaths that came before?'
stories.insight: Some true ideas are resisted because accepting them means accepting guilt for past harm.
stories.quote: he realized that indirectly without knowing it, he killed her. So he kills himself.

stories.summary: Ajay recalls the tidy childhood version of scurvy. Sailors died in agony until it turned out that carrying preserved lime fixed the problem, because all they lacked was vitamin C. But when you check the dates, decades passed between the discovery and its wider adoption.
stories.insight: Discovery is often not the bottleneck; adoption is. Even a cheap, proven fix can sit unused for a generation.
stories.quote: When you go examine the dates carefully, it's like decades went by

stories.topic: Wegener stares at a map until the continents move
stories.summary: Alfred Wegener got his idea by looking at a map. The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa fit like jigsaw pieces. He turned this into testable claims: the same fossils and the same rock formations should appear on both sides. He found both, then similar matches elsewhere, and proposed that a single supercontinent, Pangaea, had split apart. His peers asked what force could possibly move continents. His 1912 book was met with derision, and he died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. Only in the 1960s did plate tectonics win acceptance. Ajay remembers his father treating it as hot new science, including the idea that India broke off near Madagascar and smashed into Eurasia, pushing up the Himalayas.
stories.insight: The evidence was in front of everyone; it took one person to look and decades for the field to catch up. Amit adds that Wegener was no outsider but a working geologist, punished for stepping past convention.
stories.quote: Just imagine how many people would have looked at that same map.

stories.topic: Boltzmann misses his vindication by a few years
stories.summary: In the 1860s and 1870s Boltzmann helped move physics from the kinetic theory of gases, where molecules are deterministic hard dots, to statistical mechanics. It used probability throughout to link microscopic states to measurable quantities like temperature and entropy. The theory predicted well, but no microscope of the day could show an atom, so sceptics asked whether anyone had ever seen one. He struggled for jobs, was thrown out of his home university in Vienna, and killed himself in 1906. That was a couple of years before the world accepted he was right. Ajay says these stories come from Jacob Bronowski's The Ascent of Man.
stories.insight: Vindication can arrive just after the person is gone. Ajay's broader point: being a maverick is a lonely psycho-social battle against jobs, careers and an establishment, while the warm comfort is to go with the flow.
stories.quote: And it just is so unlucky that this was a couple of years before all his stuff worked out and suddenly the whole world was ready to say that Boltzmann was right.

stories.summary: Mendel was an obscure monk in Austria who tried to turn breeders' intuitions about inheritance into laws. He was lucky to choose a simple plant, the pea, and his results marked one of the great moments in science. But printing was expensive: the run for his paper was 40 copies, all he could afford, and he mailed them to a few people. Those who read it shrugged that plant breeding was nothing new, and missed what it meant.
stories.insight: The economics of distribution once decided which ideas spread. A world-changing result could be stuck at forty copies, read by people who couldn't see its importance.
stories.quote: So the print run for his paper was 40. He purchased 40 copies from the printer because that's all he could afford.

stories.summary: Darwin sailed on the Beagle collecting specimens, and by 1837, thinking about the creatures of the Galapagos, he grasped evolution. He immediately saw it as a personal disaster, because telling the world God did not create us would bring everyone down on him. So he spent some 22 years polishing his book. Meanwhile Alfred Russel Wallace, delirious with malaria in the jungles of Indonesia, cracked the same theory from scratch. Having a bias for action, he came home ready to present. Friends who knew of Darwin's secret project arranged a simultaneous presentation in 1859. Even then evolution lacked a mechanism, as critics demanded to be shown where the code of the finch was written. Only near the end of the century did people join it to Mendel's genetics, giving biology its first real theory.
stories.insight: Caution and boldness both have costs: Darwin's perfectionism nearly cost him priority, as with Newton and Leibniz. Big theories sometimes need two outlaws' halves, separated by decades, to fit together.
stories.quote: And as he understood it, he also understood this is a personal disaster.

stories.summary: In mid-nineteenth-century London, John Snow worked out that cholera spreads through water. The finding met resistance for decades, especially in India. Near the end of the century another investigator mapped cholera deaths in an Indian village and found that most victims were upper caste. They drew from a contaminated well that lower castes were barred from using. The only lower-caste victim was the washerman who washed their clothes. Amit credits Chinmay Tumbe's Age of Pandemics for the story.
stories.insight: Data can expose a society's structure as sharply as a disease's route. Here exclusion ironically protected the excluded, and even so clear a link took decades to be accepted.
stories.quote: So the only person from a lower caste who got cholera was a washerman who washed their clothes.

stories.summary: Katalin Karikó's early mRNA research was treated as a fringe joke. She applied for grant after grant and was rejected every time. The University of Pennsylvania told her she was not of faculty quality. Years later, as Amit puts it, the moment met the woman: mRNA vaccines proved a miracle, and in a sense she saved the planet.
stories.insight: Amit then turns the story around. We only hear about the outlaws who were eventually vindicated, while many others were right, ignored and never redeemed.
stories.quote: she famously said that every night I was working grant, grant, grant, and every time the reply came back, no, no, no.

stories.topic: The population column and reflexive rage
stories.summary: When Amit wrote a column arguing that population is a strength rather than a problem, many readers reacted with instant anger and abuse instead of engaging with the argument. His reading is that school had taught them population is India's problem. They had folded that belief into their identity, so they experienced his argument as an attack on themselves.
stories.insight: Once a belief becomes part of the self, disagreement feels like aggression. That is one answer to why the conventional-minded turn aggressive.
stories.quote: So if you attack any part of that package of beliefs they have adopted, you are attacking them and they will react in that manner.

recommendations.creator: Charlotte Gordon
recommendations.context: Amit calls it the first recommendation of the day; it supplied most of his material on Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley, and he reads passages from it.
recommendations.reason: A joint biography of mother and daughter that vividly shows how hostile their world was to women. Animals gained legal protection in 1824, twenty years before the first law limiting violence against women.

recommendations.item: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
recommendations.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
recommendations.context: Discussed at length; Amit reads passages and notes the show has recommended it before.
recommendations.reason: The founding protofeminist text, written with no role models. It argues that a false education makes women slaves of the male gaze, and it grounds virtue in reason rather than religion or tradition. It may read tame today, so read it against its time.

recommendations.creator: Mary Shelley
recommendations.context: The centre of the second chapter.
recommendations.reason: An eighteen-year-old wrote it with no genre and no craft models. Brian Aldiss called it the first science fiction book. Its three-narrator nested structure was innovative, and its question, whether the beings we create have rights, is live again with AI.

recommendations.item: The Book Club, Episode 2: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions the audio show he did for Storytel, talking about one book for fifteen minutes; he covered both Wollstonecraft and Shelley.
recommendations.reason: A quick audio introduction to Wollstonecraft's book from Amit himself.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The companion Storytel episode, linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: A fifteen-minute audio take on Frankenstein, to pair with the Wollstonecraft episode.

recommendations.item: The Collected Letters of Mary Wollstonecraft
recommendations.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
recommendations.context: Mentioned while telling the story of her suicide attempt; her suicide letter is reproduced there.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'a beautiful book': Wollstonecraft's inner life in her own words.

recommendations.creator: John Milton
recommendations.context: One of Mary Shelley's formative books; Amit quotes 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man?'
recommendations.reason: To see where Frankenstein's central question, a creature confronting its creator, comes from.

recommendations.creator: Denis Villeneuve
recommendations.context: Cited while arguing that science fiction tackles the biggest questions of modern times.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a magnificent meditation on the shaping of the self and the nature of memory.

recommendations.creator: Alex Garland
recommendations.context: Cited as a modern film on the same theme as Frankenstein.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it great; it asks whether something we create that approaches consciousness has rights.

recommendations.creator: Sherwin Nuland
recommendations.context: Amit promised to link books about Semmelweis in the show notes; this is the one linked.
recommendations.reason: The full story of Semmelweis: the discovery, the rejection and the tragic end.

recommendations.item: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit recalls 'an early episode on how character can be contingent' while discussing Semmelweis's later decline.
recommendations.reason: Gives a lens on how small things can make you a different person, which bears on whether Semmelweis's degeneration was illness or partly what the world did to him.

recommendations.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: Source for the John Snow and caste-cholera-map stories.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a wonderful book that tells, fascinatingly, how cholera's link to water was found and then resisted for decades, especially in India.

recommendations.creator: Jacob Bronowski
recommendations.context: Ajay says the Wegener, Boltzmann, Mendel and Darwin stories all come from it; he watched it as a child and has recommended it before.
recommendations.reason: A sweeping history of scientific thought that has shaped Ajay since childhood and is full of stories like these.

recommendations.creator: Jacob Bronowski
recommendations.context: Recommended together with the BBC series.
recommendations.reason: The written companion to the series that fed Ajay's stories of scientific outlaws.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Amit opens the chapter on the aggressively conventional-minded with it, noting it came up in the very first episode of the show.
recommendations.reason: A two-axis frame (passive vs aggressive, conventional vs independent) that identifies the aggressively conventional-minded as the real threat to new ideas. Amit calls it 'such a great frame'.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's own column, cited as the time aggressively conventional readers attacked him.
recommendations.reason: A reasoned case that population is a strength, and a live demonstration of how people react when a school-taught belief is challenged.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's population column.
recommendations.reason: The show's own fuller treatment of the argument that drew reflexive anger.

recommendations.item: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
recommendations.creator: Adam Mastroianni
recommendations.context: Amit's second essay recommendation; he had shared it on Twitter and sent it to Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Argues that most research today is super safe and nobody chases moonshots. It sets out the life cycle of new ideas: a weirdo outsider proposes one, experts ignore or suppress it, and eventually it wins because it's better.

recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen
recommendations.context: Raised while discussing Mastroianni's essay; Amit notes that Shruti runs the India branch.
recommendations.reason: Amit finds it wonderful that it funds mad ideas from people with no credentials.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay says his selection-bias argument here is 'essentially the same story we told in our Knowledge Society episode', where he discussed the five personality traits.
recommendations.reason: The fuller argument for why the academic system filters out creative mavericks.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit points out that Ajay made this filtering argument at length in their education episode too.
recommendations.reason: The same critique of conformity-selecting institutions, approached through schooling.

recommendations.item: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
recommendations.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of a great dissident who documented his own strangeness.
recommendations.reason: It shows in great detail how Gandhi was 'quite a weirdo', a reminder of how unconventional great free thinkers look up close.

recommendations.item: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's point that we only remember the sugar-coated highlights of figures like Newton and Gandhi.
recommendations.reason: An earlier episode on the same figures Ajay invokes when he warns against judging free thinkers by their highlight reels.

recommendations.context: Ajay's formal recommendation for the episode, after Amit begs him for a conventional one.
recommendations.reason: Boltzmann's grave bears his entropy equation, S = k ln W, a fitting pilgrimage to an outlaw who died just before the world caught up with him.

core_ideas.explanation: Progress is slow. In every age some people think things that will later seem completely normal but are radical at the time, and they are often shunned, despised or destroyed for it. Seen in hindsight, their stories are deeply moving.
core_ideas.quote: And in every age you find people who are ahead of their time who are thinking things which later will be considered completely normal, but at the time are radical.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's intellectual hero John Locke grounded liberalism in one premise: you own yourself. Every other right follows from it. Free speech follows because you own your thoughts, property because you mix your labour with unowned things, and life follows too. Locke himself was treated as an outlaw in his time, yet his ideas inspired the American Declaration of Independence and, through it, Wollstonecraft.
core_ideas.quote: And Locke's fundamental philosophy is this, that all of us are born with the right to self-ownership.

core_ideas.explanation: Wollstonecraft argued that humans are special because we can reason, and that virtue, which only our species has, must therefore flow from reason. It sounds bland now, but it was radical: virtue was then assumed to come from religion, tradition and convention, so her argument challenged every construct of society, not just relations between the sexes.
core_ideas.quote: Our species is special because we are capable of reason.

core_ideas.concept: Radicals must first speak their audience's language
core_ideas.explanation: Because Wollstonecraft's only readers were men who read political philosophy, she couldn't argue that women would be autonomous and fulfilled. She had to argue that freed women would be better daughters, sisters, wives, mothers and citizens. Amit finds this tragic, but it is how the first version of a radical idea gets through the door.
core_ideas.quote: And it's kinda tragic that because she is making this case to people who read works of political philosophy, which are all men, she has to do it in those terms.

core_ideas.explanation: Frankenstein looks clichéd today only because so much later work copied it. The same is true of Fritz Lang's Metropolis in cinema and of much that came from Shakespeare. When reading an originator, remember that the clichés started there.
core_ideas.quote: And here is the thing, do not judge her for those cliches because they started there. They weren't cliches there.

core_ideas.concept: Science fiction carries the biggest questions
core_ideas.explanation: Amit resists treating science fiction as a niche subgenre and counts some of the greatest writers, like Margaret Atwood and Ursula K. Le Guin, among its practitioners. Frankenstein's question was live in 1818 and is live again with AI: if we create a being that surpasses us cognitively and differs only in not being mortal or organic, why should it be our moral inferior?
core_ideas.quote: I think the biggest questions of modern times are actually tackled by science fiction.

core_ideas.explanation: The recurring reason true ideas get rejected is that they work without a known 'how'. Semmelweis had no germ theory, Wegener no force to move continents, Darwin no genetics, and Boltzmann no microscope able to show an atom. Good predictions were not enough; the establishment waited, sometimes for decades, until the last-mile explanation arrived.
core_ideas.quote: Last mile problem. Darwin did not have the explanation. So this is a recurrent theme we'll see again and again.

core_ideas.concept: Science advances one funeral at a time
core_ideas.explanation: Amit invokes the Planck principle: new ideas win not by converting their opponents but as those opponents die off. Playing the long game is cold comfort when, as Keynes said, in the long run we're all dead. Amit's open question is why science has to progress by funerals.
core_ideas.quote: It reminds me of the Planck principle, science changes one funeral at a time.

core_ideas.explanation: We celebrate Semmelweis, Wegener and Karikó because they were eventually vindicated, even if only after death. For each of them, countless others were right, ignored and never redeemed, so hero stories hide the true cost of being early. Amit guesses only one in a million make it that way.
core_ideas.quote: these are heroic and tragic stories, but there's a survivor bias here.

core_ideas.explanation: Paul Graham sorts people on two axes, conventional versus independent-minded and passive versus aggressive. The passively conventional are most common and the aggressively independent rarest. Amit sees Wallace as aggressively independent and Darwin as passively independent. Being conventional-minded is understandable, as cognitive economy or even rationality. What puzzles Amit is the aggression, which he sees as the real danger to progress.
core_ideas.quote: Graham's point, and I agree entirely with him, this is such a great frame, is that the greatest danger is from the aggressively conventional minded.

core_ideas.explanation: Social media amplifies aggressively conventional behaviour, especially in ideological tribes where attacking heretics raises your status. People get cancelled and outcast far faster than Semmelweis was. Echoing Mastroianni, Amit argues that where Wegener faced disdain only from fellow professionals, a modern Wegener would face the whole world, so few propose such ideas and research stays safe.
core_ideas.quote: Today the whole world will. And that is such a disincentive.

core_ideas.concept: Why the conventional get aggressive: defending the system
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's answer to Amit's puzzle: people are tacitly upholding an establishment of institutions, credentials, journals, universities, jobs and funding. An idea that disrupts it threatens their own lives, so they defend it like any bureaucracy. Amit's population story adds an identity angle: when beliefs fuse with the self, challenges feel like attacks.
core_ideas.quote: It's the same as any other bureaucracy. What bureaucracies want is to keep the boat going.

core_ideas.explanation: Since most people ignore mavericks, taking them seriously is a personal arbitrage opportunity. Many of their ideas will be wrong, but that is where the innovation lies. Ajay suggests spending an hour with a 'mad person' over a sane one and changing our conformist filters (clean shirt, right jokes, one of the gang). Amit adds the caveat: don't listen blindly, but do take them seriously.
core_ideas.quote: For you, for me, and for you, gentle reader, this is an arbitrage opportunity. This is a $500 bill lying on the ground.

core_ideas.concept: Creativity and weirdness are causally linked
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that a well-socialised person absorbs their elders' programming. The kind of imagination that produces a Boltzmann probably requires being somewhat badly adjusted, so not every oddball is a genius, but a disproportionate share of geniuses are oddballs. That makes them hard to accept in a society whose structures are quiet, tame and conventional.
core_ideas.quote: The very act of imagination, the very act of creativity is probably grounded in being a bit of a weirdo, in not having those same social skills, and in coming across as an oddball person.

core_ideas.concept: The career pipeline selects for conscientiousness alone
core_ideas.explanation: Every rung of an intellectual career rewards keeping your head down and playing the game: board exams, college grades, a PhD with three safe papers, an academic job, then papers and grants for tenure. Of the five personality traits, only conscientiousness gets selected. This helps explain why knowledge resourcing has grown by millions of times while progress feels underwhelming.
core_ideas.quote: So there's a selection bias that the people who flourish in the traditional institutional infrastructure of the intellectual world are just selected and filtered for a certain lack of creativity and a lack of imagination.

core_ideas.concept: Sugar-coated heroes and the modern microscope
core_ideas.explanation: We admire Newton or Solzhenitsyn through their highlights. A WikiLeaks-style dump of their lives would reveal the reckless, imprudent behaviour that comes with free thinking. Today social media and surveillance put that microscope on every living maverick, making it easy to dismiss them as madmen and damaging the innovation process.
core_ideas.quote: If you had a microscope on their lives, as we do in the modern world, on the lives of all the wonderful mavericks around us, then you're going to dismiss them and rule them out of polite company saying, oh that guy is a madman.

core_ideas.explanation: In Graham's essay, Princeton's Robert George asks his students whether, as white people in the pre-abolition South, they would have been abolitionists. They all say yes, which simply isn't true. Admiring Semmelweis or Darwin now costs nothing. The real test is whether we take today's oddballs seriously.
core_ideas.quote: But there are Darwins and Mendels around us who we probably ignore and we think of them as weird and we're not taking them seriously.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on Darwin spending 22 years on his book: 'Amitbhai, you'll be pleased to know he was as great a book writer as you.' Amit: 'He took a long time, you mean.' Ajay: 'He just plodded and plodded and plodded, and he didn't even have a word processor.' Later, at '22 years', Amit: 'I have time, I have time.'

Ajay on Wallace cracking evolution in a malarial delirium: 'Gentle reader, please hope that your creative energies are fueled by malaria... Amitbhai, you may consider getting a little malaria to assist your project.'

Ajay on Darwin's theory: 'One day we were told God created man. Next day we are told we came out of monkeys. I mean it's quite a fall.' On cartoonists drawing Darwin as a monkey: 'he had a face for that.'
Ajay on Newton sitting on the calculus while Leibniz rushed to publish: 'It's like I'm Newton. Once I understand it, how can humans understand it?'

In Washington DC, Amit's history-obsessed friend Vikram Raghavan points to a building where John Maynard Keynes had a heart attack under a staircase. Amit: 'So did he say in the short run we are all dead?' Keynes survived that one.
Amit's verdict on the roughly 4,000 words Percy Shelley contributed to Frankenstein: they stand out because they're bad writing, and Shelley's own novels are 'pretty bad'.
After Ajay says it's better to spend an hour with a mad person than a sane one, Amit: 'That's why I do the show with you.'
Amit, pulling Ajay back to his question: 'But that five hundred dollar bill as five hundred dollar bills tend to do distracted you.'

Amit pleads for a conventional recommendation, because last time Ajay told him to go to 'Huntsville, Arizona'. Ajay corrects him ('Huntsville, Alabama') and then recommends going to a place again: Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna.
Ajay: 'If biology has to be more than stamp collecting, then it is the child of Mendel and Darwin.'

Thomas Taylor's mocking reply to Wollstonecraft, 'A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes': if women get rights, why not animals? Amit notes that Peter Singer would later make the animal case seriously in Animal Liberation.
Horace Walpole's put-down of Mary Wollstonecraft: 'a hyena in petticoats.'

Edmund Burke's conservative defence of tradition and aristocracy against the French Revolution, answered by Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790); Amit notes Thomas Paine's response is better remembered.
John Locke, now the father of liberalism, was himself treated as an outlaw; Amit believes Cambridge banned him in 1701.
Brian Aldiss called Frankenstein the first book of science fiction.

The anatomist William Lawrence's no-soul lectures, relayed by John Polidori, and Percy Shelley's Promethean obsession, which later produced Prometheus Unbound: the intellectual sparks behind Frankenstein.

Fritz Lang's Metropolis, cited as the origin of many cinematic clichés, just as Frankenstein originated literary ones; Ajay adds the Shakespeare example 'All that glisters is not gold' (not 'glitters').
Margaret Atwood and Ursula K. Le Guin, Amit's examples of great writers who are science fiction writers.

Amit imagines the Wollstonecraft, Shelley and Semmelweis stories as one interlocking web series, a relay race across the dates (Frankenstein and Semmelweis both from 1818) that begins and ends with childbirth, handwashing and death.
